This Week in Democracy: Floods, Firings, and a Weaponized Federal Government

As Texas buried its dead, Washington gutted oversight, purged loyalty lists, and turned the machinery of government against critics, migrants, and dissent.

```markdown Central Texas was still counting its dead when the rest of the week's machinery began turning. Catastrophic flooding killed dozens of people and left hundreds missing, and in the days that followed, a familiar pattern emerged: the National Weather Service's warnings had been degraded by earlier staffing cuts, and a new Department of Homeland Security approval requirement delayed FEMA's search-and-rescue teams by more than three days. Rather than address the shortfall, DHS accused the media of "deliberate lying" about the disaster's causes. It was a preview of the week's dominant theme — a government stripped of capacity, then defensive about the consequences.

The weekend carried other, equally consequential news. The Supreme Court narrowed the ability of federal judges to block executive actions on a nationwide basis, a procedural shift that would ripple through nearly every legal fight against the administration for the rest of the year. Its first casualties were visible almost immediately: eight immigrants with no ties to South Sudan were deported there after a judge's authority to stop the move was curtailed by the very ruling handed down days earlier. Meanwhile, President Trump signed a sprawling reconciliation bill that made the 2017 tax cuts permanent, cut roughly $1.1 trillion combined from Medicaid and food assistance, and funneled $170 billion into immigration enforcement, including $51.6 billion for a border wall — adding an estimated $3.4 trillion to the deficit in the process. The same weekend brought a purge of national security leadership, with NSA Director Gen. Timothy Haugh and six National Security Council staffers fired after being named on lists supplied by an outside influencer, and an FBI agent resigning over what he described as political pressure and ideological screening. Trump also pardoned January 6 defendants while directing the Justice Department to investigate his critics, and Elon Musk, breaking publicly with the president over the budget bill, filed paperwork to launch a new political party.

By Monday, the Court's influence was compounding. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissed all 17 members of the CDC's vaccine advisory panel, replacing them with vaccine skeptics, while promoting unproven measles treatments and reviving a long-discredited vaccine-autism claim — actions that would draw lawsuits from medical associations and a pregnant physician within days. In Los Angeles, federal agents and National Guard troops staged a militarized raid in the MacArthur Park neighborhood, complete with armored vehicles and horseback units; no arrests were made, and local officials called it intimidation, a "reality TV spectacle" with no evident law-enforcement purpose. It was the first of several such operations that would grow more violent as the week went on. Separately, the Supreme Court allowed the administration's plan for mass federal layoffs to proceed over a sharp dissent from Justice Jackson, and in Boston, a trial opened to determine whether immigration law had been used to deport pro-Palestinian foreign students over their political speech — a First Amendment test with implications well beyond the individual defendants. The day closed with a jolt to the administration's own coalition: the Justice Department announced it had found no evidence of an Epstein client list, reversing earlier promises and triggering backlash from MAGA-aligned figures and House Democrats alike, an unusual moment of shared frustration across the political divide.

Tuesday deepened the structural story. The Supreme Court ruled that a former president holds broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts, a decision that narrows the law's reach over the nation's most powerful office. That same day, even as flood recovery continued in Texas, the administration announced plans to dismantle FEMA entirely by the end of hurricane season, arguing states and private enterprise could manage disaster response instead. A presidential memo stripped security clearances from Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, Kamala Harris, and a whistleblower attorney, prompting a lawsuit alleging unconstitutional retaliation. In San Francisco, an unmarked ICE vehicle drove through a crowd of protesters outside the immigration court, injuring at least one person, while agents used batons, pepper spray, and rifles against demonstrators with no visible police intervention. Trump floated the idea of a federal takeover of New York City should Zohran Mamdani win the mayoral race, and suggested Washington, D.C. might similarly come under direct federal control. The IRS, meanwhile, announced that churches could endorse political candidates without losing tax-exempt status, ending a seventy-year interpretation of the Johnson Amendment, and a new report showed the Pentagon budget approaching $1 trillion annually, with more than half of recent discretionary spending flowing to private contractors. Marines and National Guard troops were dispatched to Florida to support ICE operations, including a pilot program stationing agents at a Marine Corps base.

Wednesday brought the Supreme Court's third major intervention of the week, clearing the way for mass firings across nineteen federal agencies. The Justice Department sued California over its transgender athlete policies and subpoenaed more than twenty clinics providing gender-affirming care to minors. In Florida, the Miami City Commission voted to postpone its 2025 municipal election to 2026 without voter input, extending the terms of officials who would otherwise have faced reelection — a move critics called a direct assault on voters' right to choose their representatives. Trump escalated his tariff campaign, announcing a 50 percent tariff on Brazil explicitly tied to the domestic prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro, opening a trade investigation into Brazil's social media regulations, and issuing new tariffs against the Philippines, Algeria, Iraq, and other nations. ICE detained an Ohio imam whose asylum status had been abruptly terminated and separately arrested a mother of four U.S.-born children who had lived in the country since age three. Trump repeated his federal-takeover threats against New York and Washington, and Florida opened a new detention facility in the Everglades that was quickly reported to have inhumane conditions. He also signed Medicaid work-requirement legislation, with administration officials suggesting recipients could replace migrant farm labor lost to deportation — tying the week's healthcare cuts directly to its immigration crackdown.

Thursday offered the week's clearest picture of institutions adapting under pressure. A federal judge in New Hampshire blocked Trump's executive order ending birthright citizenship, certifying a nationwide class action — a narrower legal tool deployed precisely because the Supreme Court had foreclosed broader injunctions days earlier. It was a rare demonstration that courts could still constrain executive action, even after losing some of their sharpest instruments. But the same day, DHS eliminated its Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties along with two immigration ombudsman offices, removing internal oversight just as detention and enforcement were intensifying. A former DOJ attorney, Erez Reuveni, produced text messages supporting his claim that a senior Justice Department official had instructed lawyers to disregard court orders blocking deportations to El Salvador — evidence striking directly at the rule of law. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott announced plans to redraw the state's congressional map mid-decade at the Trump administration's urging, aiming to secure additional Republican seats before the midterms. Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil filed a $20 million claim alleging false imprisonment after months of detention without charges tied to his campus activism, and Rep. Jared Moskowitz renewed calls for a congressional investigation into the DHS approval rule that had delayed flood rescue teams.

The week closed on Friday with the State Department issuing termination notices to more than 1,300 employees — roughly 15 percent of its domestic staff — as part of a reorganization built around an "America First" foreign policy. In California, federal agents and National Guard troops raided cannabis farms in Carpinteria and Camarillo, arresting 200 workers and using chemical munitions on protesters; a farmworker later died from injuries sustained during the operation, the grimmest point yet in a week of escalating enforcement violence. North Carolina lawmakers advanced legislation that would replace nonpartisan election board members with partisan appointees, alongside a separate bill critics said could restrict political expression on government property. And it was confirmed that DHS had canceled a $3 million grant meant to improve communication between the National Weather Service and local officials — the same kind of infrastructure whose absence had contributed to the Texas flood death toll, cut even as search and rescue operations were still underway.

Taken together, the week traced a government reorganizing itself around loyalty, force, and diminished oversight, often while insisting nothing had gone wrong. A disaster exposed what years of quiet budget cuts had hollowed out, and the response was not reinforcement but further retrenchment — a plan to eliminate the very agency meant to answer such disasters. Courts lost some of their broadest tools to check the presidency, then improvised narrower ones to preserve constitutional guarantees, an adaptation that succeeded this week but whose durability remains untested. Security clearances, silence orders, and personnel purges were turned against critics and career officials alike, while oversight offices built to catch abuses in immigration enforcement were dismantled just as that enforcement grew more forceful and, in California, fatal. Even the administration's own coalition found reason for public anger, when a long-promised disclosure evaporated into denial. None of these developments occurred in isolation; each fed the next, and by week's end the throughline was unmistakable — a widening gap between the institutions meant to check power and the pace at which that power was being exercised. ```
